calls.reason: The Harvard study finds only modest source-quality deterioration, with low-quality link volume stable or declining. That proxy does not establish whether misinformation became substantially worse.

The Chrysidis study finds growing AI misinformation and slower initial notes, but stronger subsequent agreement. Its selected sample and the later addition of AI writers do not establish that human correction was overwhelmed.

TruthfulQA tests false-answer generation, not detection. The GPT-3 tweet study finds mixed detection performance, with uncertain experimental timing, and neither study establishes unmatched misinformation generation.

ReFACT and the political fact-checking study show persistent weaknesses, while other evaluations find gains in larger models. These mixed results establish neither a scale-only solution nor that scaling cannot deliver one.

The exponential forecast is explicitly hedged. Epoch documents falling prices, but the Harvard study chiefly tracks harmless synthetic media and does not establish misinformation growth caused by cheaper LLMs.

The October 2022 ReAct evaluation shows PaLM assessing claims using retrieved Wikipedia evidence, scoring 60.9 on FEVER. That demonstrates a way to reason against a reference standard, despite substantial reliability limits.
